disease.name: Pneumonia
disease.scientific_name: Pneumonia / Pulmonary Consolidation / Lower Respiratory Tract Infection (LRTI)
disease.icd_10_code: J18 (Pneumonia, unspecified organism); J13 (Pneumococcal pneumonia); J14 (Haemophilus influenzae pneumonia); J15 (Bacterial pneumonia NEC); J12 (Viral pneumonia); J16 (Pneumonia due to other infectious organisms); J85 (Abscess of lung); J86 (Pyothorax/Empyema); J18.9 (Unspecified pneumonia)
disease.category: Respiratory Infectious Disease / Lower Respiratory Tract Infection

overview.description: Pneumonia is an acute infectious inflammation of the lung parenchyma — specifically the alveoli (air sacs), bronchioles, and interstitial tissue — caused by bacteria, viruses, fungi, or other pathogens, and occasionally by chemical aspiration. The alveoli fill with exudate (pus, fluid, or inflammatory cells), impairing gas exchange and causing the cardinal features of fever, productive cough, dyspnoea, and lobar or multilobar consolidation on chest imaging. Pneumonia is one of the leading causes of global morbidity and mortality — the single most common infectious cause of death worldwide, killing approximately 2.5 million people per year, and the leading cause of death in children under 5 years globally (accounting for 14% of all under-5 deaths).
overview.affected_organ: Lungs (alveoli, bronchioles, interstitium); systemically in severe cases: blood, kidneys, heart, brain, and all organs (sepsis)
overview.prevalence: Approximately 450 million cases of pneumonia occur globally per year; 5-10 million hospitalizations annually in the USA alone. India: estimated 43 million episodes annually, contributing significantly to global burden. Incidence peaks at age extremes: infants/children and elderly >65 years.
overview.age_group: All ages affected; highest mortality in children <5 years and adults >65 years; immunocompromised individuals at highest risk for severe/atypical pneumonia at any age.
overview.is_contagious_note: Most pneumonias are caused by organisms spread via respiratory droplets (coughing, sneezing), aerosols, or direct contact; some are aspiration-related (not person-to-person)
overview.key_fact: Pneumococcal vaccination (PCV20/PPSV23) and annual influenza vaccination are the single most effective preventive measures — reducing pneumonia hospitalizations by 30-50%

pathophysiology.normal_lung_defense: The respiratory tract normally defends against pathogens through: mucociliary clearance (mucus trapping + ciliary sweeping), cough reflex, alveolar macrophages (resident phagocytes), secretory IgA (mucosal immunity), complement system, surfactant proteins (A and D — opsonise pathogens), and lymphocytes
pathophysiology.how_pneumonia_develops: Pneumonia develops when: (1) pathogen burden overcomes normal defenses (large inoculum); OR (2) host defenses are impaired (immunosuppression, cigarette smoking, COPD, aspiration); OR (3) pathogen has specific virulence factors that evade normal clearance. Pathogens reaching alveoli trigger activation of alveolar macrophages → inflammatory cytokine release (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-8) → neutrophil recruitment → exudate filling alveolar spaces → consolidation (hepatisation) → impaired gas exchange (hypoxia)
stages_lobar_pneumonia: Engorgement (12-24 hours): vascular congestion, alveolar oedema, bacteria begin multiplying in alveoli
Red Hepatisation (2-4 days): fibrinous exudate + red blood cells + neutrophils fill alveoli; lung solid and red (liver-like appearance)
Grey Hepatisation (4-8 days): red cells lyse; fibrin, neutrophils, and macrophages remain; lung grey and airless
Resolution (8-10 days): enzymatic digestion of exudate by macrophages; gradual restoration of normal alveolar architecture; lung clears

types.name: Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP)
types.description: Pneumonia acquired outside of hospital settings or within 48 hours of hospital admission in a patient who has not been in a healthcare facility recently. The most common type — affecting all age groups. Caused predominantly by Streptococcus pneumoniae (30-40%), but also Haemophilus influenzae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, respiratory viruses (influenza, COVID-19, RSV), and many others.

typical_vs_atypical.typical: Bacterial CAP (Streptococcus pneumoniae, H. influenzae) — abrupt onset; high fever; rigors; productive cough (rusty/purulent sputum); pleuritic chest pain; lobar consolidation on CXR; responds to beta-lactam antibiotics
typical_vs_atypical.atypical: Atypical/walking pneumonia (Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydophila) — subacute onset; dry or minimally productive cough; extrapulmonary features (headache, diarrhoea, confusion); patchy bilateral infiltrates on CXR; responds to macrolides/doxycycline/fluoroquinolones

types.severity_tool: CURB-65 score for CAP (Confusion, Urea, Respiratory rate, Blood pressure, age ≥65) guides site-of-care decisions
types.common_in: All ages; peaks in elderly >65; children <5; immunocompromised; smokers; COPD patients

types.name: Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia (HAP)
types.description: Pneumonia occurring ≥48 hours after hospital admission that was NOT incubating at time of admission. Associated with more drug-resistant organisms than CAP — gram-negative bacteria (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella, Acinetobacter, E. coli) and MRSA (Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus) predominate. Higher mortality than CAP (20-50%).
types.risk_factors_for_HAP: Prolonged hospitalisation, immobility, surgical procedures (especially abdominal/thoracic), altered consciousness, aspiration, nasogastric tube, immunosuppression, antibiotic use (selecting resistant organisms)
types.treatment: Broader-spectrum antibiotics covering gram-negatives and MRSA (piperacillin-tazobactam, ceftazidime, meropenem ± vancomycin or linezolid) — guided by local antibiogram and respiratory culture

types.name: Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP)
types.description: Pneumonia occurring ≥48-72 hours after endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. One of the most serious HAI (healthcare-associated infection). Develops from micro-aspiration of oropharyngeal secretions contaminated with bacteria around the endotracheal tube cuff. High mortality (20-40%). Organisms: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, MRSA, Acinetobacter baumannii (XDR — extensively drug-resistant), Klebsiella, gram-negative enterics.
types.prevention: VAP bundle: head-of-bed elevation 30-45°; oral care with chlorhexidine; daily sedation interruption; minimise ventilation days; subglottic secretion drainage; hand hygiene

types.name: Aspiration Pneumonia and Aspiration Pneumonitis
types.description: Aspiration PNEUMONITIS: chemical injury from aspiration of sterile gastric contents (acid, enzymes) into lungs — initial non-infective; may or may not progress to secondary bacterial pneumonia. Aspiration PNEUMONIA: infection from aspiration of oropharyngeal or gastric contents containing bacteria — common organisms are oropharyngeal anaerobes (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Prevotella, Peptostreptococcus) and gram-negatives.
types.risk_factors: Altered consciousness (stroke, anaesthesia, intoxication, seizures, drug overdose), dysphagia (neurological disease, oropharyngeal tumours, achalasia), lying flat, nasogastric tube, gastroparesis, GERD
types.typical_location: Right lower lobe (supine patients); right middle lobe — dependent on patient position at time of aspiration; bilateral if massive aspiration
types.management: Antibiotics covering anaerobes: amoxicillin-clavulanate; clindamycin + a beta-lactam; metronidazole + amoxicillin; piperacillin-tazobactam (if hospitalised and severe)

types.name: Atypical (Walking) Pneumonia
types.description: Pneumonia caused by 'atypical' organisms — so named because they do not respond to standard beta-lactam antibiotics and have clinical and radiological features distinct from typical bacterial pneumonia. Patients are often ambulatory ('walking pneumonia'). Pathogens: Mycoplasma pneumoniae (most common in young adults and school-age children), Legionella pneumophila (environmental water sources; can cause severe Legionnaires' disease), Chlamydophila pneumoniae.
types.legionella_note: Legionella pneumophila causes two distinct syndromes: (1) Legionnaires' disease — severe atypical pneumonia with high fever, confusion, diarrhoea, hyponatraemia (low sodium), elevated LFTs; mortality 5-30% (higher in immunocompromised); (2) Pontiac fever — non-pneumonic self-limiting flu-like illness. Diagnosed by urinary Legionella antigen (most practical) or culture of respiratory secretions on BCYE agar.
types.mycoplasma_note: Mycoplasma pneumoniae: gradual onset (2-3 weeks); dry hacking cough persisting weeks; associated with cold agglutinins causing haemolytic anaemia; bullous myringitis; skin rashes (erythema multiforme); CNS complications (encephalitis, meningitis)

types.name: Viral Pneumonia
types.description: Pneumonia caused by viruses directly infecting lower respiratory tract — distinct from secondary bacterial pneumonia following a primary viral URTI. Viral pneumonias typically cause diffuse bilateral interstitial patterns ('ground-glass opacity' on CT) rather than lobar consolidation. Primary viral pneumonias cause substantial morbidity and mortality.

major_viral_causes.features: Abrupt onset; high fever; myalgia; headache; non-productive cough progressing to dyspnoea; may develop rapidly to ARDS; secondary bacterial pneumonia (Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae) common and more lethal
major_viral_causes.treatment: Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) 75mg twice daily × 5 days — start within 48 hours of symptom onset for maximum benefit; continue beyond 48h for hospitalised or severe disease

major_viral_causes.features: May cause severe bilateral pneumonitis ('COVID pneumonia') with hypoxia often preceding dyspnoea awareness ('happy hypoxia'); bilateral ground-glass opacities in peripheral and basal distribution on CT; hyperinflammatory phase (cytokine storm); PE risk; endotheliitis
major_viral_causes.treatment: Dexamethasone 6mg daily × 10 days (RECOVERY trial — reduces mortality in patients requiring oxygen or ventilation); remdesivir (antivirals); baricitinib/tocilizumab (IL-6 inhibitor) for severe inflammatory phase; anticoagulation; oxygen/NIV/IMV

major_viral_causes.features: Leading cause of severe lower respiratory tract infection in infants and young children; bronchiolitis and pneumonia; also increasingly recognised as cause of severe pneumonia in elderly
major_viral_causes.treatment: Supportive (oxygen, hydration); palivizumab (prophylaxis in high-risk infants); RSV vaccine now available for adults ≥60 (Abrysvo, Arexvy — approved 2023)

major_viral_causes.features: Important causes particularly in children and immunocompromised; can cause severe lower respiratory tract disease
major_viral_causes.treatment: Primarily supportive; cidofovir (adenovirus in severe immunocompromised)

types.name: Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia (PJP / PCP)
types.description: Previously called Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia (PCP) — fungal pneumonia caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii affecting immunocompromised patients, particularly those with HIV/AIDS (CD4 <200 cells/µL), organ transplant recipients, haematological malignancies, or patients on immunosuppressive therapy (corticosteroids, chemotherapy, biologics). An AIDS-defining illness.
types.features: Subacute onset (weeks); progressive exertional dyspnoea; dry non-productive cough; low-grade fever; mild hypoxia disproportionate to clinical signs; bilateral perihilar or diffuse 'ground-glass' interstitial infiltrates on CXR (normal CXR in 10-25%); oxygen desaturation on exercise (characteristic); elevated serum LDH (non-specific but suggestive)
types.diagnosis: Induced sputum (1,3-β-D-glucan elevated); bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) with silver stain or immunofluorescence (most sensitive); serum β-D-glucan >80 pg/mL (suggestive)
types.treatment: Co-trimoxazole (TMP-SMX) as first-line — TMP 15-20 mg/kg/day + SMX 75-100 mg/kg/day IV or oral in 3-4 divided doses × 21 days; adjunctive prednisolone if PaO2 <70 mmHg (reduces ARDS risk); alternatives: pentamidine IV, clindamycin + primaquine, atovaquone

types.name: Fungal Pneumonia
types.description: Pneumonia caused by pathogenic fungi — predominantly in immunocompromised individuals but some organisms infect immunocompetent hosts in endemic geographic areas.

major_fungi.setting: Severely immunocompromised (haematological malignancy, organ transplant, prolonged corticosteroid use, COVID-19-associated)
major_fungi.features: Fever despite antibiotics; haemoptysis; pleuritic chest pain; CT: 'halo sign' (early — consolidation surrounded by ground-glass), 'crescent sign' (late)
major_fungi.treatment: Voriconazole (first-line); isavuconazole; amphotericin B; surgical resection for haemoptysis

major_fungi.features: Subacute pneumonia + CNS involvement (cryptococcal meningitis); India ink stain; cryptococcal antigen (CrAg)

major_fungi.setting: Endemic areas (Mississippi River valley, Southwestern USA); immunocompetent hosts possible
major_fungi.features: Subacute pneumonia; exposure to bat droppings (histoplasma), soil (coccidioides)

types.name: Necrotising Pneumonia and Lung Abscess
types.description: Necrotising pneumonia: a severe variant where pneumonia causes liquefaction and cavitation of lung tissue — multiple small cavities within areas of consolidation. Lung abscess: a single or multiple loculated cavities >2cm filled with pus within the lung parenchyma. Both conditions reflect more virulent pathogens (Staphylococcus aureus including PVL-positive strains, Klebsiella pneumoniae — Friedlander's type 2 — particularly in diabetics, alcoholics; anaerobes from aspiration; Streptococcus anginosus).
types.features: Productive cough with purulent/foul-smelling sputum; high fever; weight loss; night sweats; haemoptysis; air-fluid level on CXR (lung abscess); multiple small cavities (necrotising)
types.management: Prolonged antibiotics (4-6 weeks or until CXR resolves); anaerobic coverage (co-amoxiclav, metronidazole + beta-lactam, clindamycin); postural drainage; bronchoscopy; CT-guided drainage; surgical resection for refractory cases

severity_levels.name: Mild Pneumonia (CAP CURB-65: 0-1)
severity_levels.description: Pneumonia with minimal physiological disturbance; manageable at home
severity_levels.curb65: Score 0-1 (no confusion; urea normal; RR <30/min; BP normal; age <65)
severity_levels.features: Fever; productive cough; mild tachycardia; minimal dyspnoea; SpO2 ≥94% on room air; able to tolerate oral medications and fluids
severity_levels.management: Oral amoxicillin 500mg-1g three times daily × 5 days (or doxycycline as alternative); rest; adequate hydration; antipyretics; GP follow-up at 48 hours (phone or in person)

severity_levels.name: Moderate Pneumonia (CAP CURB-65: 2)
severity_levels.description: Pneumonia requiring hospital admission for observation, IV antibiotics, or supplemental oxygen
severity_levels.features: SpO2 90-94% on room air; RR 20-30/min; moderate tachycardia; bilateral or multilobar involvement; unable to maintain oral intake; comorbidities worsening
severity_levels.management: IV amoxicillin + clarithromycin (or ceftriaxone + azithromycin); supplemental oxygen (target SpO2 94-98%); IV fluids if dehydrated; daily review

severity_levels.name: Severe Pneumonia (CAP CURB-65: 3-5)
severity_levels.description: Severe pneumonia with significant physiological compromise requiring HDU or ICU-level care
severity_levels.curb65: Score 3-5; or any SMART-COP criteria met
severity_levels.features: SpO2 <90% on room air or requiring FiO2 >35%; RR ≥30/min; SBP <90 mmHg; bilateral or multilobar consolidation; confusion/encephalopathy; evidence of sepsis; requiring vasopressors; acute kidney injury
severity_levels.management: IV ceftriaxone + azithromycin OR respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin); add anti-MRSA cover if risk factors (vancomycin/linezolid); high-flow nasal oxygen or non-invasive ventilation; invasive mechanical ventilation if failing; sepsis bundle; vasopressors (noradrenaline)

severity_levels.name: Critical Pneumonia / ARDS (CAP CURB-65: 5 / HAP/VAP with MOF)
severity_levels.description: Life-threatening pneumonia complicated by ARDS, multi-organ failure, refractory septic shock, or requiring mechanical ventilation
severity_levels.curb65: Score 5; ARDS criteria (Berlin definition); multi-organ failure
severity_levels.features: PaO2/FiO2 <300 (ARDS); bilateral infiltrates not explained by heart failure; requiring invasive mechanical ventilation; vasopressor-dependent shock; AKI requiring RRT; hepatic failure; encephalopathy
severity_levels.management: Lung-protective ventilation (tidal volume 6mL/kg IBW, PEEP 5-20 cmH2O, plateau pressure <30 cmH2O, driving pressure <15 cmH2O); prone positioning ≥16 hours/day (PROSEVA trial — reduces mortality 28-day in moderate-severe ARDS by 16%); neuromuscular blockade; corticosteroids (dexamethasone for ARDS — DEXA-ARDS trial); ECMO (veno-venous) for refractory ARDS at ECMO centres

bacterial.prevalence: Most common identifiable bacterial cause — 30-40% of CAP
bacterial.typical_presentation: Sudden rigors; high fever; rust-coloured sputum; lobar consolidation; positive pneumococcal urinary antigen
bacterial.virulence: Polysaccharide capsule — 90+ serotypes; vaccine covers most disease-causing serotypes

bacterial.prevalence: 10-15% of CAP; especially in COPD, smokers, elderly
bacterial.type: Non-typeable H. influenzae predominant in adults; Hib (type b) in unvaccinated children — causes epiglottitis and meningitis

bacterial.prevalence: 5-15% of CAP; most common in children and young adults (school-age children)
bacterial.pattern: Epidemic cycles every 3-5 years; clusters in closed communities (schools, military, universities)
bacterial.diagnostics: Mycoplasma IgM/IgG serology; PCR nasal/throat swab; cold agglutinins (present in 50% — titer ≥1:64 supports diagnosis)

bacterial.source: Contaminated water systems: cooling towers, hospital hot water systems, whirlpool spas, air conditioning units
bacterial.key_clues: Hyponatraemia (SIADH); high fever; diarrhoea; confusion; raised LFTs and CK; negative urinary antigen for pneumococcus + positive Legionella urinary antigen
bacterial.treatment: Azithromycin or a fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin) — does NOT respond to beta-lactams

bacterial.features: Pharyngitis often precedes; gradual onset; laryngitis; mild systemic symptoms; responds to macrolides/tetracyclines/fluoroquinolones

bacterial.prevalence: Uncommon in CAP but important in specific populations
bacterial.risk_groups: Alcoholics; diabetics; nursing home residents; immunocompromised
bacterial.features: Lobar pneumonia; 'currant jelly' sputum (blood-tinged mucoid); upper lobe involvement; rapid destruction and cavitation; high mortality
bacterial.resistance: Hypervirulent Klebsiella (hvKP) and ESBL/KPC-producing Klebsiella are emerging global threats

bacterial.risk_groups: Post-influenza (secondary bacterial pneumonia); IV drug users; elderly; nosocomial
bacterial.features: Cavitation and lung abscess; pneumothorax; rapid progression; haematogenous dissemination
Mild-moderate pneumonia; typically follows viral URTI

organisms: Acinetobacter baumannii (XDR strains — major ICU threat)
hospital_acquired_HAP_VAP.note: HAP/VAP organisms show significantly higher rates of antimicrobial resistance — treatment guided by local antibiogram data and respiratory culture with sensitivity testing

risk_factors_for_pneumonia.detail: Children <5 years (immature immune system); adults >65 years (immunosenescence, comorbidities, impaired cough reflex, reduced mucociliary clearance)
Damages mucociliary escalator; impairs alveolar macrophage function; increases risk 2-4x; risk dramatically increases with chronic COPD

HIV/AIDS (PJP, fungal, bacterial); chemotherapy and bone marrow transplant; solid organ transplant; high-dose corticosteroids (>20mg/day prednisolone >4 weeks); biologics (TNF inhibitors, JAK inhibitors); haematological malignancy
COPD; bronchiectasis; cystic fibrosis; interstitial lung disease — impaired mucociliary clearance; structural lung damage; retained secretions
Impaired neutrophil function; impaired complement activation; higher risk of Klebsiella and Staphylococcal pneumonia; higher mortality from CAP
Impairs gag reflex (aspiration risk); suppresses neutrophil function; malnutrition; increases risk of Klebsiella, anaerobic aspiration, and pneumococcal pneumonia
Stroke; Parkinson's; dementia; dysphagia; GERD; reduced consciousness; seizures; general anaesthesia
Impairs cell-mediated immunity; reduces T-cell function; impairs phagocytic activity
Viral infection impairs mucociliary clearance and local immune defence — creates portal for secondary bacterial pneumonia (the most common cause of influenza-related death)
Lack of pneumococcal or influenza vaccination dramatically increases susceptibility to pneumonia
Close contact facilitates respiratory droplet transmission; common in urban India

symptoms.classical_presentation: The classic bacterial pneumonia presentation (particularly S. pneumoniae) begins with a single rigor (severe shaking chill) followed rapidly by fever, pleuritic chest pain, and productive cough with rusty or purulent sputum. Atypical pneumonias present more insidiously with dry cough and systemic features. COVID-19 pneumonia is notable for 'silent hypoxia' where patients may be severely hypoxic without feeling breathless.

primary_symptoms.name: Fever
primary_symptoms.description: Temperature ≥38°C — occurs in the majority of pneumonia patients. In typical bacterial pneumonia: high-grade fever (38.5-40°C) with rigors (severe shaking chills from bacteraemia). In atypical pneumonia: low-grade to moderate fever. In elderly: fever may be absent or minimal despite severe pneumonia ('afebrile pneumonia') — absent fever in the elderly is a poor prognostic sign (suggests impaired physiological response), NOT a reassuring sign.
primary_symptoms.onset: Usually acute (hours in typical bacterial); subacute (days in atypical/viral)
primary_symptoms.note: High fever with rigors (violent shaking chills) is characteristic of pneumococcal bacteraemia

primary_symptoms.name: Cough
primary_symptoms.description: A cardinal symptom — cough in pneumonia is typically PRODUCTIVE (bringing up sputum). Sputum characteristics are diagnostically important: (1) Rusty/blood-tinged sputum — classic pneumococcal pneumonia (from red cell breakdown in alveoli); (2) Yellow-green purulent sputum — any bacterial pneumonia; (3) Currant-jelly sputum (bloody, mucoid) — Klebsiella pneumoniae; (4) 'Anchovy sauce' sputum — amoebic lung abscess; (5) Dry/non-productive cough — atypical pneumonia (Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydophila) and viral pneumonia; (6) Foul-smelling — anaerobic aspiration pneumonia.

primary_symptoms.name: Dyspnoea (Breathlessness)
primary_symptoms.description: Shortness of breath on exertion progressing to rest dyspnoea as pneumonia severity increases. Results from: alveolar consolidation reducing gas exchange surface area; V/Q mismatch; reduced lung compliance; pain limiting deep breathing (pleuritic). In COVID-19 pneumonia: 'silent hypoxia' or 'happy hypoxia' — patients may be severely hypoxic (SpO2 80-85%) without subjectively feeling breathless — due to attenuated hypoxic ventilatory response. Dyspnoea at rest is an alarm sign requiring urgent hospital assessment.
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild (on exertion) to Severe (at rest, requiring supplemental oxygen)
primary_symptoms.alarm: Dyspnoea at rest or SpO2 <90% = EMERGENCY

primary_symptoms.name: Pleuritic Chest Pain
primary_symptoms.description: Sharp, stabbing, unilateral chest pain worsened by deep inspiration, coughing, or sneezing — caused by inflammation of the visceral and parietal pleura overlying the pneumonic consolidation. Highly characteristic of pneumonia (particularly lobar pneumonia) and pleuritis. May restrict deep breathing causing hypoxia. Radiates to shoulder (if diaphragmatic pleura involved — phrenic nerve distribution) or referred to abdomen in lower lobe pneumonia — potentially mimicking an acute abdomen.

primary_symptoms.name: Rigors (Shaking Chills)
primary_symptoms.description: Violent, uncontrollable shivering with teeth chattering and muscle contractions during the abrupt rise in fever — characteristic of bacteraemia (bacteria in bloodstream). A SINGLE episode of rigors at the onset of illness is highly characteristic of pneumococcal pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae). Multiple rigors suggest malaria or recurring bacteraemia. Rigors indicate the sudden massive bacteraemia characteristic of pneumococcal invasion.
primary_symptoms.severity: Severe — distressing to patient and observers
primary_symptoms.clinical_significance: One rigor at onset = classic pneumococcal pneumonia; multiple rigors = consider bacteraemia from another source or malaria

primary_symptoms.name: Systemic Features — Malaise, Myalgia, Headache
primary_symptoms.description: Systemic inflammatory response to infection: profound fatigue and malaise from cytokine release (TNF-α, IL-6); myalgia (muscle aches) from systemic inflammation — particularly prominent in influenza, Legionella, and Mycoplasma; headache from fever and possibly CNS involvement. In Legionella pneumonia: confusion, diarrhoea, and headache are particularly prominent extrarespiratory features.
primary_symptoms.onset: Concurrent with or preceding respiratory symptoms in atypical/viral pneumonia

secondary_symptoms: Haemoptysis (coughing blood) — frank blood from inflamed airways or cavitating pneumonia; small amounts common; large haemoptysis is an alarm sign (consider fungal, Klebsiella, TB, lung abscess)
Nausea and vomiting — systemic response; common in Legionella (diarrhoea prominently)
Loss of appetite — from systemic illness
Confusion and disorientation — important alarm feature (CURB-65 C criterion); indicates severity; particularly prominent in elderly and Legionella pneumonia
Tachycardia — proportional to fever and hypoxia; HR >100 bpm typical
Tachypnoea — respiratory rate >20/min (>30/min = CURB-65 criterion = severe); most reliable early sign of severity
Central cyanosis — blue discolouration of lips and tongue — severe hypoxia; late sign
Diarrhoea — prominent in Legionella (50%); also viral pneumonias (COVID-19)
Herpes labialis (cold sore reactivation) — classic trigger with pneumococcal pneumonia

physical_examination_findings.inspection: Tachypnoea; use of accessory muscles (sternocleidomastoid, intercostals); intercostal recession in children; nasal flaring; cyanosis (late); reduced chest expansion on affected side
physical_examination_findings.palpation: Increased vocal fremitus (tactile) over consolidation; tracheal deviation (tension pneumothorax — moves away from side; large effusion — moves away); reduced chest expansion
physical_examination_findings.percussion: Dullness to percussion over consolidation or pleural effusion (stony dull over fluid vs wooden dull over consolidation)
auscultation: Bronchial breathing: hollow, tubular breath sounds heard over solid consolidation (normally only at trachea); pathological when heard in the lung periphery
Crepitations (crackles): late inspiratory fine crackles (alveolar fluid) or coarse crackles (large airway secretions) — best heard after cough or deep breath
Pleural friction rub: creaking leathery sound; synchronous with respiratory movement (not heartbeat); indicates pleuritis
Reduced or absent breath sounds: over effusion or complete consolidation
Whispering pectoriloquy: whispered sounds transmitted clearly through consolidation ('99' heard clearly)
special_signs_severe_pneumonia: Confusion or drowsiness (Glasgow Coma Scale <15) — CURB-65 positive
Hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg) — CURB-65 positive; indicates septic shock
Bilateral or multilobar involvement on CXR

key_points: Children may not localise symptoms to the chest — young children present with non-specific features: fever, rapid breathing, poor feeding, lethargy

Tachypnoea (fast breathing) is the most sensitive sign of pneumonia in children — WHO respiratory rate thresholds: >50 breaths/min (<2 months); >40 breaths/min (2-12 months); >30 breaths/min (1-5 years)
Chest in-drawing (intercostal and subcostal recession) indicates severe respiratory distress in children
Coughing is variable — young infants may present with apnoea rather than cough
Fever without obvious focus in infants and toddlers — pneumonia must be excluded
RSV bronchiolitis (wheeze + respiratory distress, usually <2 years) and pneumonia may coexist
Signs of very severe pneumonia in children: inability to drink, central cyanosis, severe lower chest in-drawing, grunting respirations, altered consciousness, convulsions

alarm_signs: SpO2 <92% on room air — or requiring supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 ≥94%
Systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg (or MAP <65 mmHg) — septic shock
Confusion, disorientation, or reduced Glasgow Coma Scale — encephalopathy from hypoxia or sepsis
Heart rate >125 bpm with signs of shock
Haemoptysis (coughing blood) — lung abscess, cavitation, or malignancy
Bilateral or multilobar consolidation on CXR
Evidence of empyema or large pleural effusion
Failure to improve after 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotics — consider resistant organism, empyema, or alternative diagnosis

diagnostic_approach.clinical_diagnosis: Pneumonia is diagnosed on clinical grounds (history + examination) supported by radiological confirmation (chest X-ray). WHO clinical definition for childhood pneumonia: fast breathing ± chest in-drawing in a febrile child. For adults: new lower respiratory symptoms + fever + new radiographic infiltrate consistent with infection.
diagnostic_approach.microbiological_workup: In hospitalised patients and severe CAP: blood cultures (2 sets before antibiotics), sputum Gram stain and culture, pneumococcal urinary antigen, Legionella urinary antigen, respiratory viral PCR panel. In outpatients with mild CAP: microbiological workup not required routinely.

medical_history: Symptom onset and progression: acute (hours — typical bacterial) vs subacute (days to weeks — atypical, viral, mycobacterial, fungal)
Cough: productive or dry; sputum colour and volume; haemoptysis
Fever pattern and severity: rigors (pneumococcal bacteraemia); sweats
Dyspnoea severity: exertional or rest; progression rate
Pleuritic chest pain: laterality and radiation
Extrapulmonary features: diarrhoea (Legionella, COVID-19); rash (Mycoplasma); confusion; myalgia (atypical/viral)

Exposure history: sick contacts; travel (Legionella — hotels/cruise ships; endemic fungi — histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis); bird contact (psittacosis — Chlamydia psittaci); farm animal contact (Q fever — Coxiella burnetii); water exposure (Legionella)
Immunosuppression status: HIV (test if unknown); chemotherapy; biologics; organ transplant; corticosteroids
Aspiration risk: dysphagia; stroke; alcohol; consciousness level; recent anaesthesia
Comorbidities: COPD; asthma; diabetes; heart failure; chronic renal disease; liver disease
Vaccination history: pneumococcal vaccine; influenza vaccine; COVID-19 booster status
Recent antibiotic use (may affect culture results and guide resistance patterns)
Occupation: healthcare worker (TB, influenza, COVID-19 risk); farmer (zoonotic); construction (histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis)
physical_examination: Vital signs: temperature; heart rate; respiratory rate (most sensitive pneumonia severity marker); blood pressure (hypotension = septic shock); SpO2 (most critical parameter)
General: appearance, distress, able to complete sentences

Respiratory examination: inspection (breathing pattern, cyanosis, accessory muscle use, intercostal recession), palpation (expansion, vocal fremitus), percussion (dullness), auscultation (bronchial breathing, crepitations, pleural rub, reduced breath sounds)
Cardiovascular: HR, BP; signs of right heart failure (raised JVP, oedema) from severe hypoxia; pericardial rub
Abdominal examination: hepatomegaly (Legionella, hepatitis); tender RUQ (liver abscess); abdominal rigidity (referred pain from lower lobe pleuritis mimicking acute abdomen)
Neurological: confusion; meningism (pneumococcal pneumonia with meningitis); focal neurology
Skin: rash (measles, varicella, Mycoplasma erythema multiforme); herpes labialis (S. pneumoniae trigger); jaundice (Legionella, severe sepsis)

diagnostic_tests.description: Mandatory first-line imaging in all suspected pneumonia. Confirms diagnosis, assesses extent, identifies complications. Findings: lobar or segmental consolidation (alveolar airspace filling — appears as opacification that obscures vascular markings but often shows air bronchograms); interstitial infiltrates (viral/atypical — bilateral; perihilar or basilar); pleural effusion; cavitation (necrotising/abscess); pneumothorax. CXR may appear normal in early pneumonia and in immunocompromised patients (negative CXR does NOT exclude pneumonia if clinical suspicion is high).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm diagnosis; assess extent and severity; identify complications (effusion, cavitation, pneumothorax); guide site-of-care decision

key_findings.lobar_consolidation: Homogeneous opacification of entire lobe with air bronchograms — typical of S. pneumoniae
key_findings.bilateral_interstitial: Bilateral perihilar ('butterfly') or diffuse bilateral ground-glass — viral pneumonia, PJP, COVID-19
key_findings.patchy_bilateral: Atypical pneumonia (Mycoplasma); COVID-19 (bilateral peripheral lower zone)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: High-Resolution CT Scan of Chest (HRCT / CT Thorax)
diagnostic_tests.description: More sensitive than CXR — detects pneumonia in 10-15% of cases where CXR appears normal (immunocompromised, early disease). Essential for: suspected complications (empyema, abscess, necrotising), CXR-negative pneumonia with high clinical suspicion, failure to improve on treatment (look for unusual organisms, complications, alternative diagnoses such as malignancy or PE), COVID-19 pneumonia assessment (typical peripheral bilateral ground-glass with crazy-paving in severe COVID).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm pneumonia when CXR negative; detect complications; assess extent of COVID-19 pneumonitis; identify suspected malignancy or PE; evaluate non-resolving pneumonia
diagnostic_tests.ct_severity_index: CT severity scoring (CT-SS) for COVID-19: each of 5 lobes scored 0-5 based on % involvement; total 0-25; >18 predicts need for ICU

diagnostic_tests.description: Essential in all pneumonia patients. Leukocytosis (WBC >12,000/µL) with neutrophilia suggests bacterial pneumonia; leukopenia (<4,000/µL) indicates severe infection or viral aetiology — and carries worse prognosis. Lymphopenia is characteristic of severe COVID-19 (marker of severity). Anaemia may indicate haemolysis (Mycoplasma — cold agglutinins) or chronic disease.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess severity; guide antibiotic decisions; detect haematological complications
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: WBC >15,000/µL with band forms: bacterial pneumonia; WBC <4,000/µL: severe or viral; Lymphopenia <1,000/µL: COVID-19 severity marker; Thrombocytopenia: severe sepsis

diagnostic_tests.description: CRP: elevated in bacterial and viral pneumonia; >100 mg/L suggests significant bacterial infection; serial CRP monitors treatment response (rising CRP on antibiotics = inadequate response). Procalcitonin (PCT): most specific bacterial infection marker — elevated >0.25-0.5 ng/mL in bacterial infection; suppressed in viral pneumonia. PCT-guided protocols reduce antibiotic duration without compromising outcomes (PCT <0.25 ng/mL → withhold or discontinue antibiotics).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess severity; guide antibiotic initiation (PCT); monitor treatment response; guide antibiotic discontinuation
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: CRP >200 mg/L: severe bacterial infection; PCT >2 ng/mL: severe bacterial sepsis; PCT <0.1 ng/mL: unlikely bacterial — consider withholding antibiotics if clinical picture allows

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) or Venous Blood Gas (VBG)
diagnostic_tests.description: Essential in all hospitalised pneumonia patients and all patients with SpO2 <94% on pulse oximetry. Measures: PaO2 (partial pressure of oxygen); PaCO2 (partial pressure of CO2 — elevated indicates type 2 respiratory failure, exhaustion); pH (acidosis indicates severe disease); bicarbonate; lactate. PaO2/FiO2 ratio defines ARDS severity.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess severity of respiratory failure; identify type 1 (low PaO2, normal/low PaCO2) vs type 2 (low PaO2, high PaCO2); guide oxygen therapy and ventilation decisions
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: PaO2 <8 kPa (60 mmHg) on room air: significant hypoxaemia; PaO2/FiO2 <300: ARDS (Berlin criteria); PaCO2 >6 kPa (45 mmHg): hypercapnia (type 2 failure — exhaustion); pH <7.35: acidosis

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Blood Cultures (2 Sets Peripheral Venous — Before Antibiotics)
diagnostic_tests.description: Blood cultures should be taken from 2 separate peripheral venipuncture sites (NOT the same draw) before the first antibiotic dose. Each set contains an aerobic and anaerobic bottle. Positive in approximately 10-15% of CAP and 20-30% of severe CAP. A positive blood culture confirms bacteraemia, identifies the causative organism, and provides antibiotic sensitivity data — allowing targeted de-escalation. False-positive rates are low when proper aseptic technique is used.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identify causative bacteraemia; guide antibiotic de-escalation based on sensitivities; confirm organism in severe cases
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive culture with pathogen: confirms diagnosis; antibiotic sensitivities guide de-escalation; repeat cultures 48h if fever persists (assess clearance of bacteraemia)

diagnostic_tests.description: A GOOD QUALITY sputum sample (not saliva — must contain mucoid or purulent material; <10 squamous epithelial cells/low-power field; >25 WBCs/low-power field) is Gram-stained and cultured for bacterial identification and sensitivity. Provides organism and antibiotic sensitivity data within 24-72 hours. Sensitivity limited by prior antibiotic use and difficulty obtaining adequate sample in community practice.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identify causative organism and antibiotic sensitivities; guide de-escalation of empirical antibiotics
diagnostic_tests.sample_collection: Early morning sputum; deep cough into sterile pot; process within 2-4 hours of collection; if unable to expectorate — consider induced sputum (nebulised hypertonic saline) or bronchoscopy with BAL
diagnostic_tests.limitation: Poor sensitivity (40-60%); overdiagnoses commensal oral flora without interpretation against clinical picture

diagnostic_tests.description: Rapid, non-invasive, highly specific tests detecting bacterial antigens in urine. (1) Pneumococcal urinary antigen (BinaxNOW/Sofia): detects pneumococcal C-polysaccharide antigen; result within 15 minutes; sensitivity 50-80% for CAP; remains positive for weeks even after antibiotics started. (2) Legionella urinary antigen: detects Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1 antigen (responsible for ~85% of Legionnaire's cases); sensitivity ~70-90%; result within 15 minutes; essential for all hospitalised CAP patients.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Rapid aetiological diagnosis of two most important CAP pathogens; allows targeted therapy; does not require respiratory sampling
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive pneumococcal antigen: confirms pneumococcal aetiology → narrow to penicillin/amoxicillin; Positive Legionella antigen: confirms legionellosis → switch to azithromycin or fluoroquinolone (stop beta-lactam monotherapy)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Respiratory Viral PCR Panel (Nasopharyngeal Swab or BAL)
diagnostic_tests.description: Multiplex PCR simultaneously tests for multiple respiratory viruses (Influenza A/B, RSV, SARS-CoV-2, Adenovirus, hMPV, Parainfluenza 1-4, Rhinovirus, Coronavirus, Bocavirus) and some bacteria (Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydophila) from a single respiratory sample. Results in 1-4 hours. Essential for guiding antiviral therapy and infection control decisions.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Rapid identification of viral or atypical bacterial aetiologies; guide antiviral therapy (oseltamivir for influenza); guide infection control; support antibiotic discontinuation in viral-only pneumonia
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Influenza positive → start oseltamivir within 48h (benefit persists up to 120h in severe/hospitalised); SARS-CoV-2 positive → dexamethasone if requiring oxygen

diagnostic_tests.description: The CURB-65 score is the most widely used validated severity scoring tool for community-acquired pneumonia — recommended by BTS (British Thoracic Society) guidelines for site-of-care decisions. Calculated from 5 readily available clinical and biochemical parameters. Guides the decision between outpatient treatment, ward admission, or ICU.

parameters.C_Confusion: New onset confusion (abbreviated mental test AMT ≤8/10 or any new disorientation) — 1 point
parameters.U_Urea: Blood urea nitrogen >7 mmol/L (>19 mg/dL) — 1 point
parameters.B_Blood_pressure: Systolic BP <90 mmHg OR diastolic BP ≤60 mmHg — 1 point

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Renal Function (Urea, Creatinine, eGFR) and Electrolytes
diagnostic_tests.description: Urea (BUN) is a component of CURB-65 score. Elevated urea indicates dehydration and poor prognosis. Hyponatraemia (low sodium) is strongly associated with Legionella pneumonia (SIADH). Acute kidney injury (rising creatinine, falling urine output) occurs in severe pneumonia and sepsis.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: CURB-65 calculation; detect AKI; detect hyponatraemia (Legionella); guide fluid resuscitation; dose-adjust antibiotics (gentamicin, vancomycin)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Urea >7 mmol/L: CURB-65 positive; Na <130: Legionella strongly suggested; Creatinine rising: AKI — urgent fluid resuscitation and review nephrotoxic drugs

diagnostic_tests.description: Elevated transaminases and ALP in Legionella pneumonia (important diagnostic clue — LFT derangement in an atypical pneumonia strongly suggests Legionella). Also relevant for hepatic complications of severe sepsis, antibiotic hepatotoxicity monitoring (rifampicin, co-amoxiclav).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect Legionella (LFT elevation); assess hepatic complication of sepsis; guide drug prescribing
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: ALT/AST >2x ULN in atypical pneumonia: Legionella; Elevated ALP and bilirubin: cholestatic pattern — consider drug reaction

diagnostic_tests.description: Elevated serum lactate (>2 mmol/L) indicates tissue hypoperfusion — insufficient oxygen delivery to tissues. Essential in severe pneumonia and sepsis assessment. Lactate >4 mmol/L = septic shock regardless of blood pressure. Serial lactate monitoring guides fluid resuscitation adequacy (lactate clearance >10% in 2 hours = adequate resuscitation).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect tissue hypoperfusion and septic shock; sepsis bundle trigger (Surviving Sepsis Campaign); guide resuscitation
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Lactate >2 mmol/L: sepsis; >4 mmol/L: septic shock (start vasopressors if hypotensive); target lactate normalisation (<2 mmol/L) within 6 hours

diagnostic_tests.description: HIV testing should be offered to all patients with pneumonia where HIV status is unknown — particularly when: severe pneumonia not responding to standard antibiotics; bilateral interstitial infiltrates (PJP); young patients with severe pneumonia without apparent risk factors; recurrent pneumonia; low CD4 count suspected. PJP (Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia) is an AIDS-defining illness — prompt HIV diagnosis enables antiretroviral therapy initiation.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identify HIV-positive patients who need PJP prophylaxis and treatment; enable timely ART initiation; identify immunocompromised patients needing broader antimicrobial cover

diagnostic_tests.description: If a pleural effusion is present, diagnostic thoracocentesis (aspiration of pleural fluid) is mandatory in hospitalised pneumonia patients to exclude empyema and exudative parapneumonic effusion. Light's criteria distinguish exudate from transudate. An empyema (pus in pleural space) is a surgical emergency requiring urgent chest drain insertion.
diagnostic_tests.light_criteria: Exudate if any of: pleural:serum protein >0.5; pleural:serum LDH >0.6; pleural LDH >2/3 upper limit serum LDH
diagnostic_tests.empyema_indicators: pH <7.2; glucose <2.2 mmol/L; frank pus; positive Gram stain or culture — ANY of these: insert chest drain urgently
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude empyema (surgical emergency); characterise pleural effusion (exudate/transudate); culture pleural fluid for organism identification

diagnostic_tests.description: Bronchoscopy allows direct visualisation of airways and collection of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BAL) from the affected lobe for comprehensive microbiological analysis including: bacterial culture, fungal culture, AFB smear/culture (TB), Pneumocystis jirovecii silver stain/PCR, Legionella PCR, viral PCR. Most sensitive test for PJP (>95% sensitivity with BAL).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnosis in immunocompromised pneumonia; diagnosis of PJP; non-resolving pneumonia investigation; HAP/VAP organism identification; endobronchial obstruction (cancer, foreign body)
diagnostic_tests.indications: Immunocompromised patients with pneumonia; suspected PJP, fungal, or TB pneumonia; non-resolving pneumonia; failed empirical antibiotics

medicines.note: Antibiotic selection in pneumonia is based on: (1) setting (CAP vs HAP/VAP); (2) severity (CURB-65 score); (3) suspected causative organism; (4) local antibiogram data; (5) patient allergies and comorbidities; (6) prior antibiotic exposure. Antibiotics should be started PROMPTLY in hospitalised patients — each hour delay in severe sepsis increases mortality by 7%. All medications require prescription by a licensed physician or infectious disease specialist.

empirical_antibiotic_strategies.mild_CAP_outpatient_CURB65_0_1: Amoxicillin 1g three times daily × 5 days (first-line UK/NICE); OR Doxycycline 200mg day 1 then 100mg daily × 5 days (penicillin allergy or atypical suspected); OR Clarithromycin 500mg twice daily × 5 days (macrolide — if penicillin-allergic and doxycycline contraindicated)
empirical_antibiotic_strategies.moderate_CAP_hospital_CURB65_2: IV/oral Amoxicillin 500mg-1g TDS + Clarithromycin 500mg BD (dual therapy — beta-lactam + macrolide covers both typical and atypical); OR Doxycycline if macrolide-intolerant
empirical_antibiotic_strategies.severe_CAP_CURB65_3_or_more: IV Co-amoxiclav (Augmentin) 1.2g TDS + IV Clarithromycin 500mg BD OR IV Azithromycin 500mg OD; OR IV Ceftriaxone 2g OD + IV Clarithromycin/Azithromycin; OR IV Levofloxacin 500mg BD alone (monotherapy for non-ICU severe CAP); Add IV Vancomycin or Linezolid if MRSA suspected
empirical_antibiotic_strategies.HAP: IV Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g TDS-QDS (or TDS extended infusion over 4h); OR IV Cefepime 2g TDS; ADD Vancomycin IV (or Linezolid) if MRSA risk; ADD antifungal (anidulafungin, micafungin) in high-risk immunocompromised
empirical_antibiotic_strategies.VAP: Broader-spectrum: IV Meropenem or Imipenem (carbapenem — if ESBL or MDR organism suspected); + Vancomycin/Linezolid (MRSA); + Amikacin (if Pseudomonas suspected); guided by BAL culture within 48-72h
empirical_antibiotic_strategies.de_escalation: Review antibiotics at 48-72 hours: narrow based on culture results and sensitivities; switch IV to oral once patient improving and tolerating oral medication; typical total course 5-7 days (mild CAP); 5-10 days (moderate-severe); 14-21 days (complicated, necrotising, empyema)

categories.category_name: Beta-Lactam Antibiotics — First-Line for Typical Bacterial Pneumonia
categories.purpose: Most effective against Streptococcus pneumoniae (the most common CAP pathogen) and other gram-positive bacteria. The backbone of CAP treatment. Beta-lactams cannot cover atypical organisms — add macrolide or doxycycline for dual coverage.

medicines.name: Amoxicillin
medicines.form: Capsule, Tablet, Oral suspension, IV Injection
medicines.dosage: Mild CAP: 500mg-1g orally three times daily × 5-7 days; IV: 1g every 8 hours (hospital); High-dose: 1g TDS for severe pneumococcal or non-bacteraemic pneumonia
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE treatment for mild CAP (NICE UK guidelines); outpatient mild-moderate CAP; confirmed pneumococcal pneumonia (targeted therapy after positive urinary antigen)
medicines.mechanism: Aminopenicillin — inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis (PBP binding — prevents peptidoglycan cross-linking); bactericidal; highly active against S. pneumoniae
side_effects: Rash (maculopapular — particularly if EBV mononucleosis; not a true allergy)
Hypersensitivity (rare — anaphylaxis; ask about penicillin allergy before prescribing)
medicines.note: Does NOT cover atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydophila) — add macrolide or doxycycline when atypical pneumonia possible

medicines.name: Amoxicillin-Clavulanate (Co-Amoxiclav)
medicines.form: Tablet (625mg — amoxicillin 500mg + clavulanate 125mg), IV (1.2g — amoxicillin 1g + clavulanate 200mg)
medicines.dosage: Oral: 625mg (500/125mg) three times daily × 5-7 days; IV: 1.2g every 8 hours
medicines.use_case: Moderate-severe CAP (hospital); aspiration pneumonia (covers oropharyngeal anaerobes); beta-lactamase-producing H. influenzae or Moraxella; broad-spectrum CAP cover
medicines.mechanism: Amoxicillin + clavulanate (beta-lactamase inhibitor) — extends amoxicillin spectrum to cover beta-lactamase-producing organisms
side_effects: Cholestatic jaundice (rare but important — especially with clavulanate; avoid if prior co-amoxiclav jaundice)

medicines.name: Ceftriaxone
medicines.dosage: 1-2g IV/IM once daily (OD); 2g IV OD for severe CAP
medicines.use_case: Moderate-severe hospitalised CAP; preferred IV beta-lactam in many guidelines; excellent S. pneumoniae coverage; once-daily dosing simplifies administration
medicines.mechanism: 3rd generation cephalosporin — broad-spectrum beta-lactam; excellent CSF penetration (meningitis co-coverage if CNS involvement)

medicines.name: Piperacillin-Tazobactam (Pip-Tazo)
medicines.dosage: 4.5g IV every 6-8 hours (standard); extended infusion 4.5g over 4 hours every 6-8h (preferred for serious infections — improves pharmacodynamic target attainment)
medicines.use_case: HAP; severe CAP with Pseudomonas risk (bronchiectasis, CF, immunocompromised, prior Pseudomonas); aspiration pneumonia (anaerobic cover)
medicines.mechanism: Ureidopenicillin (piperacillin) + beta-lactamase inhibitor (tazobactam) — very broad spectrum including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, anaerobes, gram-positive and gram-negative aerobes
side_effects: Neurotoxicity at very high doses (elderly/renal impairment)

medicines.name: Meropenem / Imipenem-Cilastatin
medicines.dosage: Meropenem: 1-2g IV every 8 hours; Imipenem: 500mg-1g IV every 6-8 hours
medicines.use_case: HAP/VAP with suspected MDR gram-negatives; ESBL-producing organisms; severe HAP not responding to piperacillin-tazobactam; empirical cover while awaiting MDR culture results
medicines.mechanism: Carbapenem — broadest-spectrum beta-lactam; covers ESBL-producing organisms, anaerobes, gram-positives (not MRSA), many MDR gram-negatives
side_effects: Seizures (imipenem — CNS toxicity; use meropenem instead in patients with seizure history)
Antibiotic stewardship concern — reserve for MDR organisms; carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella (CRE) is an emerging global threat — contact infection control immediately if suspected

categories.purpose: Cover atypical pneumonia organisms (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, Chlamydophila pneumoniae) which do not respond to beta-lactam antibiotics. Used in combination with beta-lactams for hospitalised CAP to provide dual coverage (typical + atypical). Also have anti-inflammatory immunomodulatory effects.

medicines.name: Clarithromycin
medicines.dosage: Oral: 500mg twice daily × 5-7 days; IV: 500mg twice daily (switch to oral when improving)
medicines.use_case: Atypical CAP cover (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila); combination with amoxicillin/ceftriaxone for hospitalised moderate-severe CAP; Legionella (IV form)
medicines.mechanism: Macrolide — inhibits protein synthesis (50S ribosomal subunit); also inhibits H. pylori; immunomodulatory effects (reduces IL-8, TNF-α)
side_effects: QT prolongation (significant — avoid with other QT-prolonging drugs)
Drug interactions — CYP3A4 inhibitor (increases many drug levels)
contraindications: QT prolongation; concurrent QT-prolonging medications; severe hepatic failure
medicines.note: AVOID clarithromycin in pregnancy — potentially teratogenic; use azithromycin instead

medicines.name: Azithromycin
medicines.dosage: Mild CAP (outpatient): 500mg day 1 then 250mg daily × 5 days; Hospital (IV): 500mg once daily IV; Legionella: 500mg OD × 5-10 days
medicines.use_case: Atypical CAP; combination therapy with beta-lactam for moderate-severe CAP; Legionella pneumonia (IV); safe in pregnancy; daily dosing improves adherence
medicines.mechanism: Azalide macrolide — longer tissue half-life than clarithromycin (persists in tissues for 5-7 days after last dose); immunomodulatory
side_effects: Hearing loss with very high doses
medicines.advantage: Once-daily dosing; longer tissue levels (post-antibiotic effect); fewer drug interactions than clarithromycin; safe in pregnancy

medicines.name: Doxycycline
medicines.dosage: 200mg on day 1, then 100mg once daily (or 100mg BD throughout); × 5-7 days
medicines.use_case: Mild CAP — first-line alternative to amoxicillin (covers both typical and atypical organisms); penicillin allergy; atypical pneumonia including Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Legionella; Q fever (Coxiella burnetii); psittacosis
medicines.mechanism: Tetracycline — inhibits protein synthesis (30S ribosomal subunit); bacteriostatic; covers gram-positive, gram-negative, and atypical organisms
side_effects: Oesophageal irritation (take with large volume of water; remain upright 30 min)
contraindications: Pregnancy (all trimesters — bone/tooth effects on fetus)
medicines.advantage: Single agent that covers both typical AND atypical organisms — ideal for outpatient mild CAP monotherapy

categories.purpose: Fluoroquinolones specifically with potent activity against Streptococcus pneumoniae and atypical organisms — called 'respiratory fluoroquinolones'. Cover typical, atypical, and gram-negative organisms in one drug. Use reserved for severe CAP or when beta-lactam/macrolide combination not feasible.
categories.note: ANTIBIOTIC STEWARDSHIP: Respiratory fluoroquinolones should be reserved for severe/specific indications to preserve efficacy and limit resistance. They have significant side effects. Do not use for routine mild CAP.

medicines.name: Levofloxacin
medicines.dosage: Severe CAP: 500mg BD (× 5-7 days) or 750mg OD × 5 days; Legionella: 500mg BD × 10-14 days
medicines.use_case: Severe CAP (monotherapy option); Legionella pneumonia (drug of choice with azithromycin); penicillin AND macrolide allergy; CAP with multi-drug allergy; beta-lactam-allergic severe CAP
medicines.mechanism: Fluoroquinolone — inhibits DNA gyrase (GyrA) and topoisomerase IV (ParC); bactericidal; excellent intracellular penetration (atypical organisms); high oral bioavailability (oral = IV efficacy)
side_effects: Tendinopathy and tendon rupture — BLACK BOX WARNING (particularly Achilles tendon; risk higher with corticosteroids, elderly, renal disease)
QT prolongation (significant — avoid with other QT drugs; baseline ECG)
CNS effects: headache, dizziness, insomnia, seizures (elderly)

medicines.name: Moxifloxacin
medicines.dosage: 400mg once daily × 5-7 days (oral or IV)
medicines.use_case: Severe CAP monotherapy; penicillin-allergic patients with severe CAP; atypical cover; aspiration pneumonia (anaerobic cover — unlike levofloxacin); once-daily dosing
medicines.advantage: Broader anaerobic coverage than levofloxacin; once-daily dosing; high oral bioavailability
medicines.side_effects: Similar to levofloxacin; more QT prolongation than levofloxacin; avoid in cirrhosis (hepatic elimination)

categories.purpose: Cover MRSA (Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus) in pneumonia — an important cause of severe necrotising pneumonia, post-influenza pneumonia, and HAP/VAP. MRSA risk factors: HAP/VAP, IV drug use, prior MRSA infection, skin wound, haemodialysis, nursing home residence.

medicines.name: Vancomycin
medicines.dosage: 25-30 mg/kg/day IV divided every 8-12 hours; dose adjusted by trough levels or AUC monitoring
medicines.use_case: HAP/VAP with MRSA risk; severe necrotising CAP post-influenza; endocarditis with pulmonary involvement; second-line for beta-lactam-allergic patients with gram-positive pneumonia
medicines.mechanism: Glycopeptide — inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors; bactericidal against gram-positives; does NOT penetrate gram-negatives
side_effects: Nephrotoxicity (AKI — monitor creatinine and vancomycin levels closely)
Red Man Syndrome (flushing, hypotension from rapid infusion — slow infusion rate)
medicines.monitoring: Vancomycin AUC/MIC monitoring (target AUC 400-600 mg·h/L); daily renal function; trough <10 mg/L = subtherapeutic; trough >20 mg/L = toxic

medicines.name: Linezolid
medicines.dosage: 600mg IV or orally every 12 hours × 10-14 days
medicines.use_case: MRSA HAP/VAP (ADVANTAGE over vancomycin — better lung tissue penetration; comparable clinical cure rates); vancomycin failure or toxicity; complicated skin and soft tissue MRSA
medicines.mechanism: Oxazolidinone — inhibits protein synthesis by binding to 23S ribosomal RNA of 50S subunit; bacteriostatic against gram-positives; active against vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE)
side_effects: Bone marrow suppression — thrombocytopenia (monitor FBC weekly; limit to 28 days)
Serotonin syndrome (with SSRIs, MAOis — potentially fatal — contraindicated combination)
Peripheral and optic neuropathy (prolonged use >4 weeks)
medicines.advantage: Oral bioavailability ~100% (IV to oral switch possible immediately); better lung tissue penetration than vancomycin; VRE active
medicines.monitoring: FBC weekly; avoid concurrent serotonergic drugs; limit to 28-day courses; ophthalmology review if prolonged use

categories.purpose: Targeted antiviral treatment for specific viral pneumonias — primarily influenza and COVID-19.

medicines.name: Oseltamivir (Tamiflu)
medicines.dosage: Treatment: 75mg twice daily × 5 days; Severe/ICU: 75mg BD for 10 days (or longer); Prophylaxis: 75mg once daily × 10 days
medicines.use_case: Influenza A and B pneumonia (start within 48 hours of symptom onset for maximum benefit; still beneficial beyond 48h in hospitalised patients or severe disease); influenza prophylaxis (within 48h of exposure)
medicines.mechanism: Neuraminidase inhibitor — prevents viral release from infected cells and viral spread; reduces influenza severity and duration by 1-2 days; reduces pneumonia risk by 50%
side_effects: Nausea and vomiting (most common — take with food)
Neuropsychiatric events (reported in children — monitor behaviour)
medicines.dose_adjustment: Reduce dose in renal impairment (eGFR <30: 75mg OD)
medicines.note: Start EMPIRICALLY for all hospitalised patients with influenza-like illness during influenza season — do NOT wait for laboratory confirmation to initiate treatment

medicines.name: Dexamethasone (for COVID-19 Pneumonia requiring oxygen)
medicines.dosage: 6mg once daily for up to 10 days (IV or oral — equal efficacy); start ONLY when patient requires supplemental oxygen or mechanical ventilation
medicines.use_case: COVID-19 pneumonia requiring supplemental oxygen (SpO2 <92% or FiO2 requirement) or mechanical ventilation — RECOVERY Trial: dexamethasone 6mg daily reduced 28-day mortality by 17-29% in this group
medicines.mechanism: Corticosteroid — potent anti-inflammatory; reduces cytokine storm (IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1β) of COVID-19 hyperinflammatory phase; reduces lung injury progression
side_effects: Hyperglycaemia (monitor blood glucose — treat with insulin)
medicines.critical_note: DO NOT give dexamethasone to COVID-19 patients who do NOT require supplemental oxygen — RECOVERY trial showed harm (increased mortality) in this group; only give if requiring oxygen or ventilation

medicines.name: Remdesivir
medicines.dosage: 200mg IV loading dose on day 1, then 100mg IV once daily × 4 days (total 5 days)
medicines.use_case: COVID-19 pneumonia requiring supplemental oxygen but NOT mechanical ventilation; most benefit when started early in disease course; reduces hospitalisation duration by ~5 days in trials
medicines.mechanism: Adenosine analogue — inhibits viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase; broad antiviral spectrum (SARS-CoV-2, Ebola, hepatitis C)

medicines.name: Nirmatrelvir + Ritonavir (Paxlovid)
medicines.dosage: Nirmatrelvir 300mg + ritonavir 100mg twice daily × 5 days; start within 5 days of symptom onset
medicines.use_case: Mild-moderate COVID-19 at HIGH RISK of progression to severe disease (age ≥65, immunocompromised, unvaccinated, comorbidities) — reduces hospitalisation and death by 89% in EPIC-HR trial; reduces 'COVID rebound' discussed
medicines.mechanism: Nirmatrelvir: protease inhibitor of SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro) — prevents viral replication; Ritonavir: CYP3A4 inhibitor — boosts nirmatrelvir levels (pharmacokinetic booster)
side_effects: DRUG INTERACTIONS — ritonavir strongly inhibits CYP3A4 — many significant interactions including statins, immunosuppressants, anticoagulants, sedatives
medicines.critical_warning: Multiple serious drug interactions with ritonavir component — check ALL concurrent medications before prescribing; may need to hold statins, immunosuppressants for 5 days

medicines.name: Co-trimoxazole (Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole — TMP-SMX)
medicines.dosage: Treatment (severe PJP): TMP 15-20 mg/kg/day + SMX 75-100 mg/kg/day IV in 3-4 divided doses × 21 days; then oral step-down. Prophylaxis (CD4 <200): Co-trimoxazole 960mg (double-strength) once daily 3x per week or daily
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE treatment for PJP; also used for prophylaxis in HIV/AIDS (CD4 <200), organ transplant, and those on immunosuppressants
medicines.mechanism: Dual sequential block: sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase; trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase — synergistically blocks folic acid synthesis in Pneumocystis
side_effects: Bone marrow suppression (neutropenia, anaemia, thrombocytopenia — monitor FBC)
Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN (rare but serious rash — STOP immediately)
Elevated creatinine (tubular secretion inhibition — not true AKI)
medicines.adjunct: Add prednisolone 40mg BD (tapering over 21 days) when PaO2 <70 mmHg on room air — reduces mortality (NEJM 1990); prevents immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) worsening

medicines.name: Prednisolone / Methylprednisolone (Adjunct in PJP)
medicines.dosage: 40mg BD × 5 days → 40mg OD × 5 days → 20mg OD × 11 days (21-day tapering course); IV methylprednisolone 75% of prednisolone dose if patient cannot swallow
medicines.use_case: Adjunct to TMP-SMX for MODERATE-SEVERE PJP (PaO2 <70 mmHg or A-a gradient >35 mmHg); significantly reduces mortality when added to TMP-SMX in severe PJP
medicines.evidence: NEJM 1990 ACTG study: prednisolone added to co-trimoxazole reduced 84-day mortality from 37% to 11% in moderate-severe PJP; number needed to treat = 4

categories.purpose: Supportive care addressing hypoxia, fever, pain, and systemic illness — as important as antibiotics in pneumonia management.

medicines.name: Supplemental Oxygen Therapy
medicines.dosage: Target SpO2 94-98% (most patients); 88-92% (COPD/chronic hypercapnia — avoid hypercapnic drive suppression); HFNO: 20-60 L/min flow, FiO2 21-100%
medicines.use_case: ALL pneumonia patients with SpO2 <94% (or <88% in COPD); progression from nasal prongs → simple face mask → non-rebreathe mask → HFNO → NIV → IMV based on severity
medicines.mechanisms: Corrects hypoxaemia from V/Q mismatch and shunt; improves oxygen delivery to tissues; reduces cardiac work
medicines.HFNO_note: High-flow nasal oxygen (HFNO — up to 60L/min heated humidified oxygen) can avoid intubation in COVID-19 and severe CAP; a 1-hour HFNO trial (ROX index monitoring) recommended before NIV or IMV
medicines.ROX_index: ROX index = (SpO2/FiO2)/RR; ROX <3.85 at 12h on HFNO predicts failure and need for intubation

medicines.name: Paracetamol (Acetaminophen)
medicines.dosage: Adults: 1g every 4-6 hours; max 4g/day; Children: 10-15 mg/kg every 4-6 hours
medicines.use_case: Fever and pleuritic chest pain; first-line analgesic/antipyretic; safe in most patients
side_effects: Hepatotoxicity at overdose; minimal at therapeutic doses

medicines.name: Ibuprofen (NSAIDs)
medicines.dosage: 400-600mg three times daily with food
medicines.use_case: Pleuritic chest pain (anti-inflammatory effect particularly beneficial); fever; avoid in renal impairment, dehydration, and peptic ulcer disease
medicines.caution: Avoid NSAIDs in significant pneumonia (may worsen outcomes through masking fever and impairing immune response; renal impairment risk with dehydration)

medicines.name: IV Fluid Resuscitation (Ringer's Lactate / Normal Saline)
medicines.dosage: Sepsis resuscitation: 30 mL/kg IV within 3 hours; then guided by response (lactate, urine output, MAP). Maintenance: 1-2 mL/kg/hr
medicines.use_case: Dehydration from fever and reduced oral intake; septic shock (MAP <65 mmHg — vasopressors added if inadequate response to 30 mL/kg bolus)
medicines.choice: Ringer's Lactate/Hartmann's preferred over normal saline (less hyperchloraemic acidosis with large volumes)

medicines.name: Vasopressors (Noradrenaline / Norepinephrine)
medicines.dosage: 0.01-1 mcg/kg/min IV continuous infusion; titrate to MAP ≥65 mmHg
medicines.use_case: Septic shock from pneumonia — when MAP <65 mmHg despite adequate IV fluid resuscitation (30 mL/kg); first-line vasopressor in septic shock (Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
medicines.mechanism: Alpha-1 and beta-1 adrenergic agonist — vasoconstriction restoring systemic vascular resistance; positive inotropy
medicines.monitoring: Continuous arterial line blood pressure monitoring; urine output; lactate clearance

categories.purpose: Anti-inflammatory corticosteroids reduce the pathological hyperinflammatory response in certain pneumonia types. Evidence is strongest for COVID-19 and PJP. For severe CAP, evidence is emerging but not universally recommended.

medicines.name: Dexamethasone (COVID-19 — also Severe CAP)
medicines.dosage: 6mg once daily × 10 days (COVID-19 requiring oxygen); For severe non-COVID CAP — 6mg daily × 4-7 days (based on CAPE COD trial 2023 — reduces 28-day mortality in severe CAP requiring ICU)
medicines.use_case: COVID-19 requiring oxygen (RECOVERY trial); Severe CAP requiring ICU — CAPE COD trial (dexamethasone 6mg daily × 7 days reduced 28-day mortality from 26.1% to 19.3% in ICU-level severe CAP with CRP ≥150 mg/L)
medicines.evidence: RECOVERY COVID-19 trial (NEJM 2021): 6mg dexamethasone daily reduced mortality by 29% in mechanically ventilated patients; CAPE COD trial (NEJM 2023): dexamethasone reduces mortality in severe CAP

medicines.name: Voriconazole
medicines.dosage: 6 mg/kg IV every 12 hours × 2 loading doses; then 4 mg/kg IV every 12 hours; oral: 200-300mg every 12 hours
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA); also Fusarium; some Candida species; fungal pneumonia in immunocompromised
side_effects: Drug interactions — CYP2C19 metabolism; many significant interactions including tacrolimus, sirolimus, warfarin

medicines.name: Amphotericin B Liposomal (AmBisome)
medicines.dosage: 3-5 mg/kg/day IV once daily
medicines.use_case: Severe aspergillosis (voriconazole-intolerant or refractory); cryptococcal pneumonia; mucormycosis (add isavuconazole or posaconazole); endemic fungi; broad-spectrum antifungal when organism unknown
medicines.advantage: Liposomal formulation reduces nephrotoxicity vs conventional amphotericin B; broadest antifungal spectrum

medicines.name: Fluconazole
medicines.dosage: Cryptococcal meningitis/pneumonia: 400-800mg daily after amphotericin B induction; maintenance 200mg daily (lifelong in HIV until CD4 >200)
medicines.use_case: Cryptococcal pneumonia (maintenance therapy); Candida pneumonia; fluconazole-susceptible fungal infections; not active against Aspergillus (important gap)

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Nutrition plays a critical role in pneumonia recovery and prevention. During acute pneumonia, patients are often anorexic, febrile, and hypercatabolic — increasing protein breakdown and metabolic demands. Key nutritional goals are: maintain adequate hydration (thin respiratory secretions), support immune function, promote tissue healing, and prevent malnutrition-related immunosuppression. Nutritional status before pneumonia is a major determinant of outcome — malnutrition increases pneumonia severity and risk of secondary infections.

acute_phase_nutrition.hospitalised_patients: Early enteral nutrition within 24-48 hours is preferred over parenteral nutrition; nasogastric (NG) tube feeding if unable to eat orally; target 25-30 kcal/kg/day and 1.2-1.5g protein/kg/day; avoid overfeeding (increases CO2 production from carbohydrate metabolism — worsens respiratory failure)
acute_phase_nutrition.outpatients: Encourage adequate oral intake of fluids and food; start with easily digestible foods; advance as tolerated; small frequent meals

recommended_foods.category: Hydration — Critical for Respiratory Secretion Management
recommended_foods.evidence: Strong — adequate hydration thins mucus secretions, facilitating mucociliary clearance and expectoration of infected secretions

items.benefit: Adequate hydration is THE most important nutritional intervention in pneumonia. Thin mucus secretions facilitate expectoration; prevents viscous plugging; prevents dehydration from fever (600mL/day fluid loss per °C above 37°C); warm water is soothing and reduces bronchospasm
items.target: Adults: 2-3 litres daily (more if significant fever); children: 50-150mL/kg depending on age and fever
items.frequency: Sip consistently throughout day; every 15-20 minutes

items.food: Warm broths: Chicken broth, Vegetable broth, Dal soup
items.benefit: Hydration + electrolytes (sodium, potassium); protein from chicken broth (amino acids support immune function); steam inhalation effect (warm vapour moistens airways); N-acetyl cysteine-like compounds in chicken broth (mucolytic properties — documented in studies); easily digestible calories
items.frequency: Multiple times daily during acute illness

items.food: Warm herbal teas: Ginger, Turmeric, Honey-lemon, Tulsi (Holy Basil), Licorice root
items.benefit: Ginger: anti-inflammatory (6-gingerol, 8-shogaol); expectorant; anti-nausea. Turmeric (curcumin): potent anti-inflammatory (NF-κB inhibition); antiviral; antioxidant; clinical evidence for respiratory infection reduction. Honey: antibacterial (hydrogen peroxide); soothes inflamed mucosa; antioxidant. Tulsi (Ocimum sanctum): traditional Indian respiratory herb; immunomodulatory; antiviral; antifungal; reduces respiratory inflammation
items.frequency: 3-4 cups daily during illness

items.benefit: Electrolyte replacement (potassium, sodium, magnesium) lost through fever, sweating, and reduced intake; prevents hypokalaemia (common in febrile illness); gentle on stomach
items.frequency: As needed for electrolyte replacement alongside water

recommended_foods.category: Protein-Rich Foods — Immune Function and Tissue Repair
recommended_foods.evidence: Strong — adequate protein essential for immune cell production (antibodies, neutrophils, T-cells), tissue repair, and preventing malnutrition-associated immunosuppression

items.benefit: Complete protein (all essential amino acids); easily digestible; lysozyme (antibacterial enzyme in egg white); selenium and zinc (immune minerals); Vitamin D (if fortified); B12; choline (anti-inflammatory); soft texture suitable for breathless patients
items.frequency: 1-2 eggs daily during and after illness

items.benefit: High-quality lean protein; carnosine and anserine (dipeptides with anti-inflammatory effects); glutamine (essential for immune cell energy); warm chicken broth provides added expectorant effect
items.frequency: 1-2 portions daily

items.food: Fish (steamed or boiled): Salmon, Mackerel, Sardines
items.benefit: EPA and DHA omega-3 — potent anti-inflammatory; reduce cytokine overproduction (IL-6, TNF-α) that causes lung injury in severe pneumonia; improve Resolution of Inflammation (resolvins, protectins); Vitamin D (reducing respiratory infection risk); complete protein
items.frequency: 2-3 times per week

items.food: Lentils, Dal (moong dal, masoor dal), Legumes
items.benefit: Plant protein; zinc and iron (immune function); glutamine (enterocyte and immune fuel); fibre (prevents gut dysbiosis from antibiotics); easily digestible when well-cooked; moong dal khichdi is an ideal recovery food in Indian context — gentle on gut, nourishing, warm
items.frequency: Daily during recovery

items.benefit: Protein; calcium; probiotics in yogurt (restore gut microbiome disrupted by antibiotics); Vitamin D; B12; easily digestible; probiotic Lactobacillus may reduce pneumonia severity and duration (Cochrane review evidence)
items.frequency: Daily; probiotics particularly important throughout antibiotic course

recommended_foods.evidence: Strong — Vitamin C is essential for neutrophil and lymphocyte function; reduces severity and duration of respiratory infections; high-dose IV Vitamin C studied (controversially) in severe pneumonia/ARDS; deficiency dramatically impairs immunity

items.food: Amla (Indian Gooseberry) — highest Vitamin C content of any food (600-700mg/100g)
items.benefit: Extraordinary Vitamin C content; antioxidant; anti-inflammatory; antiviral; immunomodulatory; supports collagen synthesis for tissue repair. One fresh amla daily provides several times the RDA for Vitamin C
items.frequency: 1 fresh amla daily or amla juice

items.benefit: High Vitamin C (guava ~228mg/100g; kiwi ~92mg/100g); antioxidants; easily consumed when appetite is poor; anti-inflammatory polyphenols
items.frequency: 1-2 servings daily

items.benefit: High Vitamin C; lycopene (tomatoes — antioxidant); sulforaphane (broccoli — activates Nrf2 antioxidant response); easily digestible when cooked
items.frequency: Daily

recommended_foods.evidence: Strong — Vitamin D deficiency is associated with 50% increased pneumonia risk; activates antimicrobial peptides (cathelicidins, defensins) in alveolar macrophages and epithelial cells; regulates inflammatory cytokine response

items.food: Oily fish: Salmon, Mackerel, Sardines (Vitamin D + omega-3)
items.benefit: Highest dietary Vitamin D (salmon: ~600-1000 IU/100g); combined anti-inflammatory (omega-3) and immunomodulatory (Vitamin D) effects; particularly important in India where sun exposure alone may not correct deficiency
items.frequency: 2-3 times per week

items.food: Fortified milk, plant milks (Vitamin D fortified)
items.benefit: Vitamin D supplementation of milk provides significant immune support; calcium for respiratory muscle function; protein
items.frequency: Daily

items.food: Mushrooms (sun-exposed): Shiitake, Button mushrooms exposed to UV
items.benefit: Ergocalciferol (Vitamin D2) — mushrooms convert UV to Vitamin D2 when exposed to sunlight; beta-glucans in mushrooms (immunostimulant — activates macrophages and NK cells); available plant-based Vitamin D source
items.frequency: Regular

recommended_foods.category: Zinc and Selenium — Critical Immunity Minerals
recommended_foods.evidence: Strong — Zinc essential for T-lymphocyte function, neutrophil activity, and mucosal barrier integrity; Selenium critical for peroxidase enzymes reducing lung oxidative stress; both deficiencies associated with impaired immunity and increased pneumonia risk

items.benefit: Very high zinc content; antioxidant; selenium; portable snack during illness; anti-inflammatory
items.frequency: Daily handful

items.benefit: Richest food source of selenium (70mcg per nut — RDA 55mcg from just 1 nut); glutathione peroxidase activation (reduces oxidative lung injury); antiviral properties
items.frequency: 2-3 Brazil nuts daily (do not exceed — selenium toxicity possible with excess)

items.benefit: Bioavailable haem zinc; complete protein; iron (prevents anaemia worsening hypoxia); B12
items.frequency: Small portions 3-4 times per week

items.benefit: Allicin: potent natural antimicrobial (active against S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, MRSA, influenza virus); immunostimulant; antifungal; anti-inflammatory; mucolytic; sulphur compounds support glutathione (antioxidant). Evidence-based for reducing frequency and duration of respiratory infections
items.frequency: 1-3 raw cloves or heavy cooking use daily

items.benefit: Curcumin: inhibits NF-κB (master inflammatory transcription factor); reduces IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1β (key pneumonia inflammatory mediators); antiviral; antifungal; antioxidant. Piperine in black pepper increases curcumin bioavailability by 2000%
items.frequency: Daily: 1-2 tsp turmeric in warm milk (golden milk) or cooking + pinch black pepper

items.benefit: Broad-spectrum antimicrobial (hydrogen peroxide; methylglyoxal in Manuka); soothes inflamed throat and cough; antioxidant; anti-inflammatory; WHO recognises honey as effective cough relief in children; inhibits several respiratory pathogens
items.frequency: 1-2 teaspoons daily in warm water or tea; avoid in infants under 12 months (botulism risk)

items.benefit: 6-gingerol: anti-inflammatory, expectorant (loosens mucus), bronchodilator (mild), antiviral; anti-nausea (beneficial when fever causes nausea); traditional respiratory medicine with modern pharmacological evidence
items.frequency: Fresh ginger (1-2cm) in tea, food, or soup daily

items.food: Steam inhalation (hot water with eucalyptus oil or plain)
items.benefit: Warm steam moistens airways and loosens mucus; eucalyptus oil (1,8-cineole) has proven mucolytic, bronchodilatory, and anti-inflammatory effects; facilitates expectoration; reduces nasal congestion
items.frequency: 2-3 times daily during acute illness

recommended_foods.evidence: Moderate-strong — gut-lung axis is bidirectional; gut microbiome dysbiosis (from antibiotics) increases susceptibility to secondary respiratory infections; Lactobacillus supplementation associated with reduced pneumonia duration and severity in meta-analyses

items.food: Plain yogurt (curd) with live cultures, Kefir
items.benefit: Probiotics restore gut microbiome disrupted by antibiotics (ampicillin, amoxicillin, clarithromycin, fluoroquinolones — all disrupt microbiome); Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium modulate lung immunity via gut-lung axis; reduce antibiotic-associated diarrhoea; enhance secretory IgA production
items.frequency: Daily throughout antibiotic course and 4-6 weeks after
items.note: Take probiotics 2 hours apart from antibiotic doses — simultaneous administration may reduce probiotic survival
